route.note: planned on a map, not yet played in the real game

goals.title: The lab
goals.plain: A small Python toolbox starts the Minecraft server with no game window, sends it commands, resets it, shuts it down and times every step.
goals.why: Every experiment after this one needs a server we can start and wipe from a script, safely.
goals.done_when: A script can boot, command, reset and stop the server, and no server is left running afterwards.

goals.title: Talking to the server
goals.plain: The toolbox learns the server's remote-command language (RCON) so a script can type commands into the server.
goals.why: Without it nothing can place blocks or generate chunks on purpose.
goals.done_when: A script can log in and get an answer back, and a wrong password is refused.

goals.title: Build RCON messages
goals.plain: Turn a command into the exact bytes the server expects, and turn the server's bytes back into text.
goals.why: A single wrong byte and the server ignores us, so the format is checked first against the written spec.
goals.done_when: The login and command messages come out byte for byte as the spec says.

goals.title: RCON client on a fake server
goals.plain: A client logs in, sends commands and joins long answers, tested against a pretend server that we control.
goals.why: We can test refusals and very long answers instantly, without waiting 20 seconds for the real game.
goals.done_when: A wrong password is refused and a reply over 4096 bytes arrives whole.

goals.title: Running the server
goals.plain: The toolbox starts a private copy of the server, waits until it says it is ready, resets the world and always shuts it down.
goals.why: A reset in about 20 seconds makes every experiment start from the same empty world.
goals.done_when: Boot, reset and stop all work, each is timed, and no Java process is left behind.

goals.title: Private server copy
goals.plain: Copy the server jar and settings into a scratch folder, turn the remote commands on with a random password and a free port, and never touch the original folder.
goals.why: The original server folder stays exactly as it is, and each copy can run beside another.
goals.done_when: The copy has RCON on, a long random password and its own port, and the original files are unchanged.

goals.title: Stop politely, then force
goals.plain: Ask a program to stop, wait a set time, and kill it if it ignores us.
goals.why: A stuck server would otherwise sit on our small memory for good.
goals.done_when: A stubborn test program is gone within the time limit.

goals.title: Start and wait for Done
goals.plain: Start the server with a 1 GB limit and no window, and wait until its log says Done.
goals.why: This is the first moment the server can be used, and the time to get there is a number we report.
goals.done_when: The server prints Done within 60 seconds and answers the list command.

goals.title: Reset to an empty world
goals.plain: Stop the server, delete its world, and start it again so nothing from before survives.
goals.why: Every experiment must start from the same blank world or its numbers mean nothing.
goals.done_when: A block placed before the reset is gone after it, and no Java process is left running.

goals.title: Time and memory of the lab
goals.plain: Measure how long boot and reset take and the most memory the server uses, and save the numbers.
goals.why: The earlier memory number was one sample, and the plan for how many servers to run at once depends on the peak.
goals.done_when: A results file holds boot seconds, reset seconds and the peak memory in megabytes.

goals.title: No game files in our repo
goals.plain: A check walks the whole repository and fails if it finds the server program, a world file or a server settings file.
goals.why: The game files belong to someone else, so none may ever be committed.
goals.done_when: The check passes on the repo and fails on a copy that has a jar or a region file in it.

goals.title: Many worlds per gigabyte
goals.plain: Memory is the limit, so the lab measures which way of making many fresh worlds gives the most worlds per minute for each gigabyte: several ordinary servers, or many worlds inside one game process the way speedrunners do.
goals.why: The order experiment needs dozens of fresh worlds, and the cheaper way to get them saves hours; this is a measured choice and not a belief.
goals.done_when: Both ways have saved numbers (or a stated reason one could not run), and a choice file names the winner.

goals.title: Several ordinary servers
goals.plain: Run one, two and three of our private servers at once, resetting each over and over for three minutes, and count fresh worlds per minute and memory per world.
goals.why: This is the baseline route and needs nothing new to be downloaded.
goals.done_when: The results file holds worlds per minute, total memory and memory per world for one, two and three servers.

goals.title: What is installed already
goals.plain: List, without downloading or changing anything, whether the owner's game folder already holds a 1.16.1 client, the Fabric mod loader, a mods folder and the right Java.
goals.why: Whether the many-worlds route can start at all depends on this, and the answer is read, not remembered.
goals.done_when: The results file says found or missing for each item, and the game folder is unchanged.

goals.title: Many worlds in one game
goals.plain: Measure worlds per minute and memory per world with the speedrunner mods that prepare several worlds inside one game process; it downloads nothing until the owner approves the file list, and otherwise records exactly why it is blocked.
goals.why: Several worlds sharing one process could beat several servers per gigabyte, but this route needs a game window and downloads, so it must not hold anything else up.
goals.done_when: The results file holds the measured numbers, or says blocked with the reason.

goals.title: Choose the route
goals.plain: Read the saved numbers and pick the route with more worlds per minute for each gigabyte, falling back to ordinary servers whenever the other route is missing or blocked.
goals.why: One file tells every later experiment which route and how many workers to use.
goals.done_when: Made-up numbers give the right winner, a blocked or missing route falls back to ordinary servers, and the real choice file is saved.

goals.title: Run jobs on several workers
goals.plain: Hand a list of build orders to the chosen workers, never more than three servers at once, and get the results back in the order the jobs were given.
goals.why: The order experiment gets its dozens of worlds faster, and it can use either route without being rewritten.
goals.done_when: With pretend workers the results come back in job order, one worker failing is reported, and asking for four servers is refused.

goals.title: The chunk reader
goals.plain: A Python reader opens the world files the server saved and says which block sits at any position.
goals.why: The experiments compare blocks, so the reader must be right before any number is believed.
goals.done_when: The reader returns exactly the blocks we placed with commands on a live server.

goals.title: Reading one region file
goals.plain: The reader learns to open a region file, unpack the data format and turn a slice of a chunk into block names.
goals.why: These are the steps every later read depends on.
goals.done_when: Hand-built region files and slices read back exactly.

goals.title: Read the NBT format
goals.plain: Read the nested data format (NBT) the game saves chunks in: named values, lists and arrays of numbers.
goals.why: Everything in a world file is stored in this format.
goals.done_when: A hand-built sample with a compound, a list and a long array reads back exactly.

goals.title: Open a region file
goals.plain: A region file holds up to 1024 chunks; find which are present and unpack one chunk's bytes.
goals.why: This is how we know which chunks the server has built.
goals.done_when: A made-up region file with two chunks lists exactly those two and unpacks one.

goals.title: Unpack a 16-block slice
goals.plain: Turn one slice of a chunk (a palette of block names plus packed numbers) into 4096 block names, using the 1.16 packing where numbers never straddle two values.
goals.why: Version 1.16 changed the packing, and the old layout silently gives wrong blocks.
goals.done_when: Hand-packed slices with 5-bit and 6-bit entries unpack to the exact blocks.

goals.title: Block at any position
goals.plain: Ask for the block at x, y, z, including negative coordinates, plus a chunk's build status, with missing chunks answering nothing.
goals.why: Negative positions are where reading mistakes hide, and the build status shows if a chunk is finished.
goals.done_when: Positions in chunk minus one and at slice edges read right, and a missing chunk answers none.

goals.title: Using the reader
goals.plain: The reader reads a whole box of blocks, and is proven on the live server.
goals.why: A reader is only trusted after it reads back what the game itself wrote.
goals.done_when: A box fingerprint is stable and five placed blocks are read back right.

goals.title: Read a box of blocks
goals.plain: Read every block in a box and fingerprint it, so two boxes can be compared quickly.
goals.why: The order experiment compares boxes of blocks and a fingerprint tells at once if they match.
goals.done_when: The same box read twice gives the same fingerprint, and one changed block changes it.

goals.title: Proof on the live server
goals.plain: Place five known blocks with commands, save, stop, and check the reader finds every one of them.
goals.why: This is the only proof that the reader sees what the game really wrote.
goals.done_when: All five placed blocks, including a negative position and a slice edge, are read back right.

goals.title: The next-chunk lever
goals.plain: Find out whether anything the player does before a chunk is built changes what that chunk holds, starting with the order the chunks are built in.
goals.why: This is goal one: a move made before a chunk exists that changes the chunk, measured on the real game.
goals.done_when: A results file says, with counts, whether building order or a player edit changed any block, and whether it moved diamonds.

goals.title: Build chunks and compare them
goals.plain: The tools, the one-at-a-time building, the first pair and the wider search over orders.
goals.why: This is the order experiment itself, from smallest step to widest search.
goals.done_when: Every order is built, compared and counted, and the control is zero.

goals.title: Measuring tools
goals.plain: Two small tools: one finds every block that differs between two builds, the other counts ores.
goals.why: Every claim in this branch is a count made by these tools.
goals.done_when: Both tools give the right counts on hand-made examples.

goals.title: Find differing blocks
goals.plain: Compare two block maps and list every position whose block changed, appeared or vanished.
goals.why: Zero or not zero differing blocks decides the whole order question.
goals.done_when: Three planted differences are found and identical maps give an empty list.

goals.title: Count the ores
goals.plain: Count diamond, iron, coal, gold, lapis, redstone and emerald blocks in a box, chunk by chunk.
goals.why: The aim is more diamond, so diamond must be counted per chunk.
goals.done_when: A hand-made box with known ores gives the exact counts per chunk.

goals.title: Building chunks one at a time
goals.plain: The lab builds chosen chunks one after another, far from the world spawn, and waits for each to finish before asking for the next.
goals.why: If two chunks are built at once the order is not ours, so the order experiment would mean nothing.
goals.done_when: Chunks come out in the order we gave, and a neighbour of a finished chunk is still half built.

goals.title: Wait until a chunk is built
goals.plain: Ask the server to hold a chunk loaded, then keep asking whether bedrock is there until the answer is yes or time runs out.
goals.why: This is how one chunk is finished before the next is requested.
goals.done_when: A pretend server that says not yet three times and then yes makes it wait, and a timeout is reported.

goals.title: Spawn is not in the way
goals.plain: The server builds a big area around spawn at start; check that a chunk thousands of blocks away is not built until we ask.
goals.why: If spawn already built our test chunks, the order would be the server's and not ours.
goals.done_when: The far chunk is absent from the saved files before we ask and finished after.

goals.title: A neighbour is only half built
goals.plain: Build one chunk, then read the status of its neighbour in the saved files.
goals.why: Building a chunk makes the neighbours partly, which is why order could matter.
goals.done_when: The neighbour exists but its status is not full.

goals.title: Run one build order
goals.plain: Given a list of chunks, build them in exactly that order on a fresh world and return the blocks of the whole area.
goals.why: Everything after this is a comparison of such runs.
goals.done_when: A run of two chunks returns both chunks as finished with the full box of blocks.

goals.title: The first pair
goals.plain: The smallest honest experiment: one pair of neighbour chunks built A then B and B then A, with a control that repeats one order.
goals.why: One pair is cheap, and the control says whether a difference could be noise.
goals.done_when: The control shows zero differing blocks, and the pair has an exact count.

goals.title: Same order twice
goals.plain: Build A then B twice on fresh worlds and count the differing blocks; this must be zero or the test is too noisy to use.
goals.why: If the same order differs from itself, nothing later can be trusted; if so, mask the moving water and lava and run it again before going on.
goals.done_when: The count is zero, or the leftover differences are listed and masked.

goals.title: A then B against B then A
goals.plain: Build the pair in both orders and count the differing blocks; zero means this pair has no lever, and more pairs are tried next.
goals.why: Differing blocks here would be the first proof that building order changes a chunk.
goals.done_when: The results file holds the exact count of differing blocks and where they are.

goals.title: More orders and places
goals.plain: If the pair showed nothing, widen the search: every order of four chunks in a square, then more squares far apart.
goals.why: One pair at one place proves little; all 24 orders at three places is a fair test of the order idea.
goals.done_when: Every order of every square is tallied, and the number of differing blocks is exact, even if zero.

goals.title: List the 24 orders
goals.plain: Write down every order in which four chunks of a square can be built, and start the empty not-run table that the later runs fill in.
goals.why: The experiment must not miss or repeat an order, and an unfilled table must read as not run.
goals.done_when: There are 24 orders, all different, each with the four chunks, and the starter table says not run.

goals.title: All 24 orders, first square
goals.plain: Build the square in all 24 orders, compare each with the first, and tally the ores per chunk for every order.
goals.why: This is the main table: how many blocks and how many diamonds change with the order.
goals.done_when: The results file has 24 rows with differing-block counts and ore counts.

goals.title: Two more squares
goals.plain: Repeat all 24 orders on two other squares far from the first.
goals.why: A lever that exists only at one place would not help a speedrun.
goals.done_when: The results file holds 48 more rows from two other squares.

goals.title: What to do with the answer
goals.plain: The player-edit lever, the aim at diamonds and the verdict that closes goal one.
goals.why: These steps turn the measured counts into an answer, whichever way they came out.
goals.done_when: The edit lever is tested, the aim says aimed or no lever, and the verdict is written.

goals.title: The player edit lever
goals.plain: If the order did nothing, test the other lever: blocks the player broke or placed in a finished chunk before its neighbour is built.
goals.why: A player can do this in the real game, so it is the next place to look.
goals.done_when: Cells outside the edit are counted as changed or not, against a no-edit control.

goals.title: Edit commands
goals.plain: Turn a list of blocks to break or place into server commands that only touch finished, loaded chunks.
goals.why: A command into an unloaded chunk would build it early and spoil the order.
goals.done_when: The commands are right for a break and a place, and one into an unloaded chunk is refused.

goals.title: Edit then build the neighbour
goals.plain: Build chunk A, break blocks near its edge, build chunk B, and count changed cells outside the edit against a run with no edit.
goals.why: Changed cells outside the edit would mean the player shaped the next chunk.
goals.done_when: The results file holds the count of changed cells outside the edit and where they are.

goals.title: Aiming at diamonds
goals.plain: Only if something differed: find the order that gives a chosen chunk the most diamonds, and check it holds up; if nothing differed, these steps must say no lever.
goals.why: This is the owner's sketch: a move before the chunk is built that gives it more diamond.
goals.done_when: The result says aimed with a repeatable gain, or says no lever.

goals.title: Pick the best order
goals.plain: Given a table of orders and diamond counts, pick the order with the most diamonds in the target chunk, or say there is no lever when all counts are equal.
goals.why: Both answers must be correct, because a zero result is a result.
goals.done_when: A table with a clear best picks it, and an all-equal table answers no lever.

goals.title: Aim on the real table
goals.plain: Run the picker on the real tables and save the answer, with the average over all orders next to it.
goals.why: The gain only means something against the average order.
goals.done_when: The file says aimed with the best count and the average, or says no lever.

goals.title: Repeat the best order
goals.plain: Build the chosen order twice on fresh worlds; the diamond count must match the table both times, or the difference was noise.
goals.why: A gain that does not repeat is not a gain.
goals.done_when: Both repeats give the table's count, or the file says nothing to repeat.

goals.title: Does it work on a new place
goals.plain: Take the rule found on the first squares and try it on a square it never saw, against that square's average.
goals.why: A rule that only works where it was found cannot be used in a run.
goals.done_when: The rule's diamonds beat the average at the new square, or the file says it did not.

goals.title: The verdict
goals.plain: One file states what is alive and what is dead for goal one, with every claim tied to its limits.
goals.why: A no must be as exact as a yes, and no solver can answer every question about Minecraft, so each claim says its bound.
goals.done_when: The verdict file matches the result files and names the next route for anything dead.

goals.title: Write the verdict
goals.plain: Turn the result files into plain statements that each name the seed, area, height and number of orders, say not run for missing files, and give the next route for a dead lever.
goals.why: Every claim then carries its own bound.
goals.done_when: Made-up result files give the right alive, dead and not-run statements with the bounds and a reroute.

goals.title: Verdict on the real results
goals.plain: Run the verdict writer on the real result files and save the file the website reads.
goals.why: This is the single answer to goal one.
goals.done_when: The saved verdict repeats the exact counts in the result files.

goals.title: The fastest run
goals.plain: Read real seed 7 terrain with the new reader, then race the round 1 planner against the round 1 plain search on it in game ticks; playing the route in the real game with a bot is a later round.
goals.why: This is goal two: a fastest route on the real map, beating a simple baseline in game ticks.
goals.done_when: On the real map the planner finishes in fewer ticks than the plain search, with numbers saved.

goals.title: Real terrain as a grid
goals.plain: The real world, 3D, is flattened into the flat grid the solver already understands, and checked against the live game.
goals.why: The solver and the real game meet here, so a mistake here ruins every route.
goals.done_when: A real area of seed 7 is a grid file, and sampled squares match the live server.

goals.title: The flat file both languages agree on
goals.plain: Python flattens the terrain and writes a grid file, and Rust reads the very same bytes back.
goals.why: Python writes and Rust reads, so one shared sample stops them drifting apart.
goals.done_when: The bytes Python writes equal the saved sample, and Rust reads the sample's squares correctly.

goals.title: Flatten columns
goals.plain: Turn each column of blocks into one square: tree if a log stands there, water, iron if ore is within six blocks below, a stone wall if the ground jumps two blocks, else open ground.
goals.why: The solver is flat, so this rule is a stated model, and it is tested so it can be changed.
goals.done_when: A made-up landscape gives the expected tree, water, iron, wall and open squares.

goals.title: Write the grid file
goals.plain: Write the squares in the byte format the Rust grid reads, and keep one tiny sample file both languages must agree on.
goals.why: Python writes and Rust reads, so one shared sample stops them drifting apart.
goals.done_when: The bytes Python writes equal the saved sample file, byte for byte.

goals.title: Rust reads the grid
goals.plain: The round 1 Rust grid reader loads the shared sample file and gives the right size and squares; no new Rust library is needed.
goals.why: If Python and Rust ever disagree about the file, this test fails first.
goals.done_when: Loading the shared sample gives the right size and the right squares.

goals.title: Area export script
goals.plain: A script turns a box of real blocks into a grid file using the flattening rule and the grid writer, with the area (64 by 64 squares around spawn) written down in one place.
goals.why: The export logic is checked on made-up blocks before it ever touches the real world.
goals.done_when: A made-up box of blocks becomes the expected grid bytes.

goals.title: Export a real seed 7 area
goals.plain: Build an area of the real seed 7 world, read it, and save it as a grid; it must have open ground, a tree, stone and iron, or the area is widened.
goals.why: This is the real map the race is run on.
goals.done_when: The grid file exists and contains a start square, a tree, stone and iron.

goals.title: Check squares on the live server
goals.plain: Pick random squares from the grid and ask the running server what block is really there.
goals.why: This tests the flattening rule against the game, not against our idea of it.
goals.done_when: Every sampled square agrees with the live server.

goals.title: The race on real terrain
goals.plain: The round 1 planner races the round 1 plain move-counting search on the real grid, from one start and then from many starts.
goals.why: Beating a fair simple rival, with the control, is the proof the planner is any good.
goals.done_when: The planner is never slower, and its wins are counted.

goals.title: Pick a start and a finish
goals.plain: Choose a start square near the middle and a finish square next to the nearest iron, on any grid, so every race uses the same rule.
goals.why: Fixed rules for start and finish keep the race fair and repeatable.
goals.done_when: On a hand-made grid the start and the finish are the squares worked out on paper.

goals.title: Wall trap map
goals.plain: On a map with a short wall and a long way round, the round 1 plain search digs the wall and the planner walks round in fewer ticks.
goals.why: This shows on a small map exactly why planning in ticks beats counting moves.
goals.done_when: The planner's ticks are lower than the plain search's on the trap map.

goals.title: Race on seed 7
goals.plain: Run both on the real seed 7 grid from one start and save the ticks of each.
goals.why: This is the first real result for goal two.
goals.done_when: The planner's ticks are not above the rival's, and the file records both numbers.

goals.title: Race from many starts
goals.plain: Repeat the race from twenty different start squares and count the wins, ties and losses.
goals.why: One start can be luck; twenty show if the planner really is faster.
goals.done_when: Zero losses in twenty starts, with the number of strict wins saved.

goals.title: The website shows round 2
goals.plain: A web page shows the round 2 goals in plain words and the experiment's numbers, and says not run yet for anything not measured.
goals.why: The owner watches the project here, and the numbers must be the real ones.
goals.done_when: The page at http://127.0.0.1:7740/r2.html shows every goal and the real experiment numbers.

goals.title: Build the round 2 data
goals.plain: A script merges the fellows' plain-English files for round 2 with each goal's status into one data file.
goals.why: The page reads one file, the same way round 1 does.
goals.done_when: Goals from two chart files are merged by id and a goal without a status shows pending.

goals.title: Pull in the experiment numbers
goals.plain: The same script copies the numbers from the result files into the data file, and a missing file is marked not run, never zero.
goals.why: A missing result shown as zero would look like a finding.
goals.done_when: With no result files every number says not run, and with files the counts are copied exactly.

goals.title: The round 2 page
goals.plain: A page draws a card for every goal and one bar for every build order showing its differing-block count.
goals.why: A bar chart of counts per order is the picture of the experiment.
goals.done_when: The page reads the data file and has a card hook per goal and a bar hook per order.

goals.title: Serve the page
goals.plain: The existing local web server returns the round 2 page at its address.
goals.why: The owner opens it in a browser, so it must load.
goals.done_when: A request to the page on a free local port returns it.

goals.title: Link from the main page
goals.plain: The round 1 page gets one link to the round 2 page.
goals.why: One door between the two pages.
goals.done_when: The main page contains a link to r2.html.

goals.title: No server left running
goals.plain: The test makes a lab run crash and hang on purpose, then checks that no Minecraft server is still running and the port is free.
goals.why: A forgotten server eats a gigabyte of memory and blocks the next run.
goals.done_when: No server process and no held port after done, crash and stuck runs.

goals.title: Only its own folder is deleted
goals.plain: The reset step is asked to delete your real server folder and a random folder; it must refuse both and only clear its own scratch world.
goals.why: Reset means deleting a world, so a wrong path could destroy real files.
goals.done_when: Both bad paths are refused and the scratch world is cleared.

goals.title: Memory gate before starting
goals.plain: The lab is told memory is low, or three servers are already running, and must refuse to start another.
goals.why: Servers and builds share 16 GB, and running out would freeze the computer.
goals.done_when: Low memory and a fourth server are both refused.

goals.title: Only finished chunks are read
goals.plain: A hand-made chunk marked half-finished and a missing chunk are read; both must come back as unknown, not air.
goals.why: Chunks next to a loaded one are only partly made, and reading them as air would fake a difference.
goals.done_when: Half-made and missing chunks are reported unknown in every case.

goals.title: Edge blocks read back exactly
goals.plain: Blocks are placed at chunk borders, at negative coordinates, and at the lowest and highest heights, then read back after a save.
goals.why: A reader that is wrong at the edges would invent differences exactly where chunks meet.
goals.done_when: Every placed block reads back as the same block.

goals.title: No Minecraft files in the repo
goals.plain: The test scans the repo for region files, the server jar and world saves, and checks the ignore list blocks them.
goals.why: Minecraft's files are not ours to publish, and the repo should stay small.
goals.done_when: The scan finds zero Minecraft files and the ignore rules are present.

goals.title: Only block types are compared
goals.plain: Two worlds that differ only in timestamps, lighting or height maps are compared and must show zero differences; one changed block must show exactly one.
goals.why: The question is about blocks, and other saved data changes every run.
goals.done_when: Data-only changes give 0 and a single block change gives 1.

goals.title: Same order twice comes first
goals.plain: The report builder is given an order comparison with no repeat of the same order and must refuse to say order matters; if the repeat differs, it labels the result shaky.
goals.why: If the same order disagrees with itself, no difference between orders can be believed.
goals.done_when: No verdict without a same-order repeat, and shaky is flagged.

goals.title: Waiting time is not order
goals.plain: The same order is saved after a short wait and after a long wait on the real server, and the blocks are compared.
goals.why: Water and sand keep moving after a chunk is made, which could look like an order effect.
goals.done_when: The two saves give the same blocks, or the number that differs is reported.

goals.title: Is the lever a player move
goals.plain: Each step in a claimed lever is tagged as a player action or an admin command, and any admin command makes the lever lab-only.
goals.why: Commands like forceload are not moves in a real run, so a lever that needs them is no use for a speedrun.
goals.done_when: Admin-only levers are labelled lab-only and player ones are not.

goals.title: More diamonds must replay
goals.plain: A claimed gain is replayed twice in fresh worlds with the found order and compared with the default order from the same session.
goals.why: A single lucky count would be mistaken for a lever.
goals.done_when: Both replays match the claimed count and the default count is recorded.

goals.title: Real routes obey the real rules
goals.plain: Routes on the real terrain are replayed by a separate checker; mining iron with a wooden pickaxe or none must be rejected.
goals.why: A route that breaks the game's rules is not a speedrun.
goals.done_when: Every route passes the checker and the trap route is rejected.

goals.title: Lava is not floor
goals.plain: Every block name in the seed 7 area must have a known meaning, and lava, water and unknown names must never count as walkable floor.
goals.why: A route across lava looks fast on paper and ends the run.
goals.done_when: No unmapped block name and no unsafe block counted as floor.

goals.title: The edge of the map is a wall
goals.plain: A route that steps outside the area we read must be rejected.
goals.why: We know nothing outside the area, so leaving it would invent shortcuts.
goals.done_when: The route using unknown cells is rejected.

goals.title: The rival route finder is fair
goals.plain: Both route finders get the same terrain and the same budget, and on a small crop the rival must find the true best route.
goals.why: Beating a weak rival proves nothing.
goals.done_when: The rival matches the true best route on the crop with a large budget.

goals.title: Website numbers come from files
goals.plain: The test changes a saved result file and the page must change; a missing file must show not measured, never zero.
goals.why: Zero differing blocks is a real answer, so a missing result must not look like it.
goals.done_when: The page follows the file and a missing result reads not measured.

goals.title: Route shown as not yet played
goals.plain: The page must say the route was planned on the map and has not been played in the game.
goals.why: Ticks on paper are not a finished speedrun, and the site should not suggest they are.
goals.done_when: The unplayed label is on the page next to the route numbers.

goals.title: Three squares per server start
goals.plain: Instead of repeating all 24 build orders on two more squares one server restart at a time, each of the 24 runs builds all three squares far apart. That is 24 restarts, not 72.
goals.why: Each restart costs about 20 seconds and 1 GB of the small memory, so the wider test fits in minutes.
goals.done_when: The plan has exactly 24 server starts for 72 square runs, with every square's own order kept and the squares far apart.

goals.title: Guess the best order from pairs
goals.plain: Each pair of neighbour chunks may add or remove diamonds depending on which is built first. A small sum-of-pairs model is fitted from a few runs and predicts every other order.
goals.why: Four chunks have 24 orders but nine have 362,880; the pair model needs about 37 runs for nine, so aiming scales past a square.
goals.done_when: On a made-up table the model predicts unseen orders exactly, picks the best one, and says so when the table is not a sum of pairs.

goals.title: Use the spawn area as it boots
goals.plain: The server already builds a big area around the world spawn while it starts. The route is planned on that area, where a real run begins, with no extra build commands.
goals.why: The fastest run starts at spawn, so planning there is both cheaper and the true starting map.
goals.done_when: After a plain boot the reader finds a start square, a tree, stone and iron in the spawn area.

goals.title: Numbers read live
goals.plain: The page reads the experiment's result files when it opens instead of copying them in a build step. A missing file shows not run.
goals.why: A copied number can go stale after a reset and look like a finding; a live read cannot.
goals.done_when: With no result files every number says not run, and a changed file shows its new number at once.

goals.title: How tightly neighbours depend on each other
goals.plain: The 24 build orders of four chunks become a table of how much each chunk changes when the order changes, plus one number for how strongly neighbours lean on each other.
goals.why: One number says whether order is a real lever or noise, and which neighbouring pairs carry it.
goals.done_when: On made-up tables the script gives zero for no dependence and a known value for a planted one.

goals.title: How far one change reaches
goals.plain: After one change, a swapped build or one placed block, the script counts the blocks that differ at each chunk distance and says whether the damage grows or dies out.
goals.why: It shows whether a move before a chunk builds can only touch its neighbour or spread further.
goals.done_when: On a made-up chain with known decay the script reports the right counts per distance and the right growth rate.

goals.title: Is the ground really fractal
goals.plain: The script measures how rough seed 7's ground is at different distances and checks whether a straight line fits the numbers.
goals.why: The word fractal is used only if the measurement earns it.
goals.done_when: On made-up ground with known roughness the fitted slope matches, and on seed 7 the fit quality is reported.
